hook.text: A database query takes 200ms. The same query cached in memory returns in 1ms. That's the power of caching.

buildup.text: A cache stores frequently accessed data in a faster storage layer, reducing the need to fetch from the source.

discovery.text: CPU caches, browser caches, CDN caches, and Redis all apply the same principle at different layers.

twist.text: Caches introduce stale data. The cached version might not match the source. Consistency is the trade-off.

climax.text: Caching is the single most impactful performance optimization in system design.

punchline.text: Store it closer, serve it faster.

quiz.question: What is the main trade-off of caching?

hook.text: A cache hit returns data instantly. A cache miss forces a slow trip to the database. Hits are gold.

buildup.text: Hit rate is the percentage of requests served from cache. A 95% hit rate means only 5% hit the database.

discovery.text: Even a 1% improvement in hit rate can dramatically reduce database load at scale.

twist.text: A cold cache has 0% hit rate. After a restart, all requests hit the database simultaneously — a cold start storm.

climax.text: Monitoring hit rate is the most important metric for any caching layer.

punchline.text: High hit rate means the cache is doing its job.

quiz.question: What is a cache cold start storm?
options: All requests hit the database after a cache restart
Too many items are stored in cache

hook.text: Your cache holds 10,000 items but an 11th arrives. Which item gets kicked out to make room?

buildup.text: Eviction policies decide which items to remove: LRU (Least Recently Used), LFU (Least Frequently Used), or FIFO.

discovery.text: LRU evicts the item that hasn't been accessed longest. It works well for most workloads.

twist.text: LRU fails for scan-heavy workloads: one full table scan evicts all your hot data and pollutes the cache.

climax.text: No eviction policy is universal. The right one depends on your data's access patterns.

punchline.text: Eviction decides what stays in cache and what leaves.

quiz.question: What does LRU eviction do?
options: Removes the item that hasn't been accessed for the longest time
Removes the most recently used item

hook.text: A CPU register responds in 1 nanosecond. RAM takes 100ns. Disk takes 10 million ns. A 10 million-fold gap.

buildup.text: The memory hierarchy arranges storage by speed and cost: registers, L1-L3 cache, RAM, SSD, and HDD.

discovery.text: Each level is bigger but slower. L1 cache is 64 KB at 1ns. RAM is 64 GB at 100ns. The trade-off is universal.

twist.text: Programs that access memory sequentially are fast because CPUs prefetch adjacent cache lines automatically.

climax.text: Understanding the memory hierarchy explains why caching works at every level of system design.

punchline.text: Faster storage is smaller. Bigger storage is slower.

quiz.question: Why is the memory hierarchy important?
options: Each level trades speed for capacity — caching exploits this
All storage types are equally fast
It only matters for hardware design

hook.text: A cached product price is $29.99. The real price changed to $24.99 an hour ago. The cache is lying.

buildup.text: TTL sets an expiration time on cached data. After the TTL expires, the cache fetches fresh data.

discovery.text: Short TTLs keep data fresh but increase load on the origin. Long TTLs reduce load but risk staleness.

twist.text: When millions of items expire at the same TTL, the origin gets hit with a stampede of simultaneous requests.

climax.text: Adding jitter — randomizing TTLs slightly — prevents cache stampedes and smooths out refresh load.

punchline.text: TTL balances freshness and load — add jitter to prevent stampedes.

quiz.question: Why should TTLs include jitter?
options: To prevent millions of cache entries from expiring simultaneously

hook.text: The application checks the cache first. On a miss, it queries the database and stores the result in cache.

buildup.text: Cache-aside (lazy loading) puts the application in control of what goes into the cache and when.

discovery.text: Only requested data is cached. Unused data never wastes cache space. It's the most common caching strategy.

twist.text: Cache-aside can serve stale data. The database might change, but the cache won't know until the TTL expires.

climax.text: Cache-aside is simple, flexible, and works for most read-heavy applications out of the box.

punchline.text: Check cache, miss, fetch, store — the simplest pattern.

quiz.question: How does the cache-aside pattern work?
options: App checks cache; on miss, queries DB and stores result in cache
Cache writes directly to the database

hook.text: Every write goes to the cache AND the database simultaneously. The cache is always in sync.

buildup.text: Write-through ensures the cache always has the latest data. No stale reads, ever.

discovery.text: It pairs well with cache-aside: writes update both, reads always hit a fresh cache.

twist.text: Write-through adds latency to every write. Both the cache and database must confirm before returning.

climax.text: Write-through is ideal when data consistency matters more than write speed.

punchline.text: Write to cache and database together — always consistent.

quiz.question: What is the downside of write-through caching?
options: Every write is slower because both cache and DB must confirm

hook.text: Writes go to the cache only. The cache asynchronously flushes to the database in the background.

buildup.text: Write-behind (write-back) makes writes blazing fast because only the cache is updated immediately.

discovery.text: The cache batches multiple writes into one database operation, reducing database load significantly.

twist.text: If the cache crashes before flushing, recent writes are lost. Durability is sacrificed for speed.

climax.text: Write-behind is powerful for write-heavy workloads but requires accepting the risk of data loss on crash.

punchline.text: Write to cache now, flush to database later — fast but risky.

quiz.question: What risk does write-behind caching introduce?
options: Data loss if the cache crashes before flushing to the database

hook.text: The application asks the cache for data. If missing, the cache itself fetches from the database. Not the app.

buildup.text: Read-through abstracts the data source away. The application only talks to the cache, never the database directly.

discovery.text: This simplifies application code. The cache layer handles all the miss-fetch-store logic internally.

twist.text: Read-through caches need configuration for each data type. They're less flexible than cache-aside.

climax.text: Read-through is ideal when you want the cache to manage its own data lifecycle automatically.

punchline.text: The cache fetches data on miss — the app doesn't need to know.

quiz.question: How does read-through differ from cache-aside?
options: The cache itself fetches from the database on a miss, not the app
The app always queries the database

hook.text: You deploy a new cache. For the first 10 minutes, every request is a miss. Response times are terrible.

buildup.text: Cache warming preloads popular data into the cache before it starts serving traffic.

discovery.text: Warm from access logs: load the most frequently requested keys based on recent traffic patterns.

twist.text: Warming too aggressively wastes memory on data that may not be requested. Warm only the hot subset.

climax.text: Cache warming turns a cold start from a disaster into a smooth transition.

punchline.text: Preload hot data before traffic arrives.

quiz.question: What is cache warming?
options: Preloading popular data into the cache before serving traffic

hook.text: Redis does caching, message queues, leaderboards, sessions, and rate limiting — all in under 1 millisecond.

buildup.text: Redis is an in-memory data store supporting strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets, and streams.

discovery.text: Its single-threaded event loop avoids lock contention, handling 100,000+ operations per second per core.

twist.text: Redis is single-threaded. CPU-heavy operations like KEYS * block the entire server during execution.

climax.text: Redis is the most popular caching layer in the world, used by Twitter, GitHub, and Stack Overflow.

punchline.text: In-memory, blazing fast, endlessly versatile.

quiz.question: Why is Redis single-threaded?
options: To avoid lock contention and simplify the event loop

hook.text: Memcached is pure key-value caching. Redis is a full data structure server. Same category, different tools.

buildup.text: Memcached is multi-threaded and excels at simple string caching with predictable performance.

discovery.text: Redis supports complex data types, persistence, replication, and Lua scripting — far beyond simple caching.

twist.text: For pure string caching at massive scale, Memcached can outperform Redis due to its multi-threaded architecture.

climax.text: Most teams choose Redis for its versatility. Memcached wins only when pure cache throughput is the sole concern.

punchline.text: Memcached for simplicity, Redis for versatility.

quiz.question: When might Memcached outperform Redis?
options: Pure string caching at massive scale due to multi-threading

hook.text: Your Redis instance holds 100 GB. You need 500 GB. One server can't hold it all.

buildup.text: Cache sharding distributes keys across multiple cache nodes using consistent hashing.

discovery.text: Each node holds a subset of keys. The client hashes the key to determine which node to query.

twist.text: Multi-key operations like transactions or set intersections don't work across shards. Data locality matters.

climax.text: Redis Cluster handles sharding automatically with 16,384 hash slots distributed across nodes.

punchline.text: Shard the cache to scale beyond one machine.

quiz.question: What is the main limitation of cache sharding?
options: Multi-key operations don't work across shards
It's slower than a single node
It requires more memory per node

hook.text: A popular cache key expires. 10,000 concurrent requests all miss and hit the database simultaneously.

buildup.text: A cache stampede (thundering herd) occurs when many requests for the same key arrive during a cache miss.

discovery.text: Lock-based prevention: one request fetches while others wait. Probabilistic refresh: refresh before expiry.

twist.text: Serving slightly stale data during refresh is often acceptable and avoids the stampede entirely.

climax.text: Stampede prevention is critical for high-traffic systems. Without it, a cache miss can cascade into a database outage.

punchline.text: One request refreshes; the rest wait or get stale data.

quiz.question: How can you prevent a cache stampede?
options: Lock-based fetch where one request refreshes and others wait

hook.text: You update a user's name in the database. The cache still shows the old name. Which is correct?

buildup.text: Cache inconsistency occurs when the cache and database disagree about the current state of data.

discovery.text: Delete-on-write: delete the cache key on write, forcing the next read to fetch fresh data from the database.

twist.text: Race conditions still exist: a read between the DB write and cache delete can re-cache stale data.

climax.text: Perfect cache consistency is impossible without distributed transactions. Acceptable staleness is the practical goal.

punchline.text: Delete on write, accept brief staleness.

quiz.question: What is the delete-on-write pattern?
options: Delete the cache key on write so the next read fetches fresh data

hook.text: You visit a website twice. The second time, images load instantly. Your browser cached them locally.

buildup.text: Cache-Control headers tell browsers what to cache and for how long: max-age, no-cache, immutable.

discovery.text: Immutable assets with content hashes (app.abc123.js) can be cached forever — the hash changes on updates.

twist.text: Over-caching HTML pages can serve stale content for hours. HTML should use no-cache with ETags for revalidation.

climax.text: Browser caching is free performance. Proper Cache-Control headers can eliminate most repeat network requests.

punchline.text: Cache assets forever; revalidate HTML on every visit.

quiz.question: Why should immutable assets have long cache times?
options: Their content hash changes on updates, so stale versions are never served

hook.text: Your browser has a cached page. Is it still fresh? Instead of downloading again, it asks: has this changed?

buildup.text: Conditional requests use If-None-Match (ETag) or If-Modified-Since headers to check for changes.

discovery.text: If unchanged, the server returns 304 Not Modified — no body, just a confirmation. Bandwidth saved.

twist.text: Generating ETags for dynamic content adds server-side computation. For static files, the web server handles it.

climax.text: Conditional requests save bandwidth and latency by transferring data only when it has actually changed.

punchline.text: Ask if it changed — skip the download if it didn't.

quiz.question: What does a 304 Not Modified response mean?
options: The cached version is still valid; no need to download again

hook.text: A user hovers over a link. The browser quietly starts loading that page before they even click.

buildup.text: Prefetching loads resources that are likely needed next. Preloading loads critical resources earlier.

discovery.text: Preload fonts and hero images to prevent layout shifts. Prefetch the next page for instant navigation.

twist.text: Aggressive prefetching wastes bandwidth and server resources if users don't visit the predicted pages.

climax.text: Preload what's certain, prefetch what's likely. Don't waste resources on the unlikely.

punchline.text: Load resources before the user asks for them.

quiz.question: What is the difference between preloading and prefetching?
options: Preloading is for critical current resources; prefetching is for likely future ones

hook.text: Google ranks websites partly on three metrics: LCP, INP, and CLS. They measure real user experience.

buildup.text: LCP measures how fast the largest visible element loads. INP measures responsiveness to interactions.

discovery.text: CLS measures visual stability — how much the page shifts while loading. Nobody likes clicking a moving button.

twist.text: Lab scores can be perfect while real user metrics are poor. Field data from real devices is what matters.

climax.text: Core Web Vitals quantify user experience. Optimizing them means optimizing what users actually feel.

punchline.text: Fast, responsive, stable — the three pillars of web UX.

quiz.question: What does CLS measure?
options: How much the page layout shifts while loading
How quickly the page responds to clicks

hook.text: A user visits the homepage but downloads JavaScript for all 50 pages. 90% of that code is wasted.

buildup.text: Code splitting breaks the JavaScript bundle into smaller chunks. Only the needed chunk is loaded per page.

discovery.text: Dynamic imports — import('./module') — let the browser load code only when a feature is actually used.

twist.text: Too many small chunks create waterfall loading: each chunk triggers another fetch. Balance chunk count and size.

climax.text: Code splitting reduces initial load time by delivering only what the user needs right now.

punchline.text: Load only the code the user needs right now.

quiz.question: What does code splitting do?
options: Breaks JavaScript into smaller chunks loaded on demand

hook.text: There are two hard things in computer science: cache invalidation and naming things.

buildup.text: Invalidation means telling the cache that data has changed and the old version should be discarded.

discovery.text: With one cache, it's simple. With CDN edges in 200 cities, database caches, and browser caches — it's a nightmare.

twist.text: Invalidating too aggressively tanks hit rates. Invalidating too slowly serves stale data. Both are wrong.

climax.text: Cache invalidation is hard because it requires coordinating state changes across distributed caching layers.

punchline.text: Knowing when to discard cached data is the hardest problem.

quiz.question: Why is cache invalidation difficult?
options: It requires coordinating across multiple distributed caching layers

hook.text: A product price changes. Instead of waiting for the TTL, the database publishes a change event to invalidate the cache.

buildup.text: Event-driven invalidation uses message queues or change data capture to notify caches of data changes.

discovery.text: PostgreSQL's LISTEN/NOTIFY or Debezium can stream database changes to cache invalidation consumers.

twist.text: Events can be delayed, duplicated, or lost. The cache might still serve stale data for a brief window.

climax.text: Event-driven invalidation is faster than TTL but adds infrastructure complexity and delivery guarantees to manage.

punchline.text: Database changes trigger cache invalidation in near real time.

quiz.question: How does event-driven cache invalidation work?
options: Database changes publish events that trigger cache deletion
The cache checks the database periodically

hook.text: Instead of invalidating a cache key, change the key itself. Old key dies naturally; new key fetches fresh data.

buildup.text: Append a version or hash to cache keys: user:42:v3 instead of user:42. Bump the version on changes.

discovery.text: This avoids invalidation entirely. The old entry expires via TTL; the new version is a fresh cache miss.

twist.text: You still need to store the current version somewhere. If that lookup is slow, you've moved the problem, not solved it.

climax.text: Version-based keys are elegant for cache layers where direct invalidation is impossible, like CDNs.

punchline.text: Don't delete old keys — just stop asking for them.

quiz.question: How do version-based cache keys work?
options: The key includes a version that changes on updates, making old keys unused
Keys are encrypted with a version number

hook.text: You fix a typo on your website. The CDN still serves the old page from 200 edge servers worldwide.

buildup.text: CDN purging sends invalidation requests to all edge nodes to discard cached content.

discovery.text: Cloudflare can purge globally in under 150ms. Others take minutes to propagate across all PoPs.

twist.text: Purging by URL is precise but slow for bulk changes. Purging everything is fast but destroys your hit rate.

climax.text: Cache tags let you purge all resources with a specific tag — like all product images — without purging everything.

punchline.text: Purge precisely — don't nuke the entire CDN cache.

quiz.question: What are cache tags used for in CDN purging?
options: Purging groups of related resources without clearing everything

hook.text: The cache entry expired. Do you make the user wait while you fetch fresh data? Or serve stale data instantly?

buildup.text: Stale-while-revalidate serves the expired cached data immediately and refreshes in the background.

discovery.text: The user gets an instant response. The next request gets the fresh version. Perceived latency is zero.

twist.text: For rapidly changing data, the stale version might be significantly wrong. Not suitable for financial data.

climax.text: Stale-while-revalidate is the best of both worlds for content where freshness is nice but speed is critical.

punchline.text: Serve stale instantly, refresh in the background.

quiz.question: What does stale-while-revalidate do?
options: Serves expired cached data instantly while refreshing in the background
Blocks until fresh data is ready

hook.text: A single slow query runs 10,000 times per hour. Optimizing it from 500ms to 5ms saves 1,375 hours of compute per day.

buildup.text: EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows exactly where time is spent: sequential scans, nested loops, sorts, or hash joins.

discovery.text: Adding the right index, rewriting a subquery as a JOIN, or limiting result sets can speed queries 100x.

twist.text: The fastest query is the one you don't run. Caching query results eliminates database load entirely.

climax.text: Query optimization is the highest-leverage performance work. One fix can improve the entire application.

punchline.text: Find the slowest query and fix it — biggest bang for the buck.

quiz.question: What tool shows where a database query spends time?

hook.text: Each database connection costs 5-10 MB of RAM. A thousand connections consume 10 GB just for connections.

buildup.text: Connection pooling maintains a pool of open connections. Requests borrow and return them instead of creating new ones.

discovery.text: PgBouncer pools PostgreSQL connections, allowing thousands of app instances to share a handful of DB connections.

twist.text: Setting the pool too small starves the application. Too large overwhelms the database. Tuning requires load testing.

climax.text: Connection pooling is essential for any application that scales beyond a single server.

punchline.text: Share connections — don't create one per request.

quiz.question: What does PgBouncer do?
options: Pools PostgreSQL connections so many app instances share a few DB connections

hook.text: Your server can handle 10,000 requests per second. At 15,000, all requests slow to a crawl. Everyone suffers.

buildup.text: Load shedding deliberately drops excess requests to protect the capacity for the remaining ones.

discovery.text: Returning HTTP 503 to 5,000 users is better than giving all 15,000 users a terrible 30-second response.

twist.text: Smart load shedding prioritizes: serve paying customers, drop health checks, shed low-priority background tasks.

climax.text: Load shedding is the controlled sacrifice of some traffic to save the experience for the rest.

punchline.text: Drop some requests to serve the rest well.

quiz.question: What is load shedding?
options: Deliberately dropping excess requests to protect remaining capacity

hook.text: A producer sends messages faster than the consumer can process. The queue grows until memory runs out.

buildup.text: Back pressure is when a slow consumer signals the producer to slow down, preventing overload.

discovery.text: TCP does this naturally: if the receiver's buffer is full, the sender pauses until space frees up.

twist.text: Unbounded queues mask the problem temporarily but eventually crash. Bounded queues enforce back pressure.

climax.text: Systems without back pressure grow unstable under load. Back pressure is the safety valve that keeps them alive.

punchline.text: Slow down the producer before the consumer drowns.

quiz.question: What does back pressure prevent?
options: A fast producer overwhelming a slow consumer

hook.text: You optimize a function from 10ms to 1ms. But it's called once per request and the database takes 400ms. Wasted effort.

buildup.text: Profiling reveals where time is actually spent. Flame graphs show the call stack and time per function.

discovery.text: Amdahl's Law: optimizing something that's 1% of total time can never improve total performance by more than 1%.

twist.text: The bottleneck shifts. Fix the database and now the network is slow. Performance is a moving target.

climax.text: Always profile first. Optimize the actual bottleneck, not the part you think is slow.

punchline.text: Measure first, optimize the real bottleneck.

quiz.question: Why should you always profile before optimizing?
options: To find the real bottleneck instead of guessing
